The Paris Office, announced in March 2026 and to
be located at the World Bank Group’s Paris office,
will support training activities and strengthen
connections with State officials, legal practitioners, and
organizations in the region and beyond. Paris has long
been one of the Centre’s most active hearing venues.

held at the World Bank Group Paris Conference Centre,

As part of the Knowledge Bank, ICSID produces and
shares knowledge that actively contributes to the
development and modernization of international
investment law and dispute settlement.

Of all
the in-person hearings in fiscal 2026, 44 percent were
held at ICSID’s hearing center in Washington, D.C., with
the remainder taking place at venues agreed upon by
the parties: Paris (30 percent), London (12 percent),
Singapore (5 percent), and other locations (9 percent).
ICSID continued to see a diverse pool of arbitrators,
conciliators, and committee members in fiscal 2026.

cases, the second highest number in a single fiscal

and 29 percent of all appointments were nationals from
low- or middle-income economies. First-time appointees
accounted for 8 percent of all appointments; among
them, 25 percent were nationals of low- or middleincome economies and 35 percent were women.

speaking 22 languages, providing professional legal, administrative, and financial
services across all cases.

standards in case management.

The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) supports cross-border
investment by offering an independent, specialized forum for the resolution of disputes. Effective,
impartial dispute resolution strengthens confidence among investors and States and enhances
predictability — core pillars of a favorable investment landscape.

on the Settlement of Investment Disputes between
States and Nationals of Other States. This multilateral
agreement, also known as the ICSID Convention, was
formulated in 1965 by the Executive Directors of the
World Bank.
ICSID is essential to the World Bank Group’s work to
accelerate job creation at scale, a strategy focused on
investing in the physical and human infrastructure
that people and businesses need to thrive, supporting
business-enabling environments, and mobilizing
private capital.

maximize profit but rather to earn enough income to
ensure the long-term financial capacity necessary to
sustain its development activities. Allocable net income
in fiscal 2026 was $2.3 billion, and out of this, the
Executive Directors approved the allocation of
$1.1 billion to the General Reserve, and recommended
to the Board of Governors an allocation of $750 million

recommended to IBRD’s Board of Governors the

IBRD Trust Fund for Gaza and West Bank, $100 million
to the Grant Facility for Project Preparation, and
$100 million to the IBRD Surplus-Funded Livable Planet
Fund. As part of its lending, borrowing, and investment
activities, IBRD is exposed to market, counterparty,
country credit, and operational risks.

question: How long do contract-based arbitrations at ICSID take on average compared with the overall caseload?

results.text:
In fiscal 2026, ICSID published its first in-depth study on
contract-based investment dispute resolution, drawing
on an analysis of 175 cases registered under the ICSID
Convention and Additional Facility. The background
paper examines how contract-based dispute resolution
has worked in practice at ICSID, serving as both an
analytical guide and practical reference for investors,
States, and State entities. Key findings show that
contract-based arbitrations at ICSID are more timeefficient than the overall caseload, averaging 40 months
from registration to conclusion compared to 47, and
settle or discontinue at a higher rate, 43 percent versus
34 percent. The paper is accompanied by a special
issue of the ICSID Caseload – Statistics featuring data on
contract-based cases.

Two issues of the ICSID Caseload – Statistics were also
released. Published every six months in English, French,
and Spanish, this publication offers a comprehensive,
data-driven overview of all cases registered and
administered by ICSID since 1972, serving as a key
resource for practitioners and policymakers to track
trends and developments in international investment
dispute settlement.
Visit icsid.worldbank.org/resources/
publications to download and read all ICSID
publications.
CASE MANAGEMENT AND
DISPUTE RESOLUTION
ICSID administers investment disputes arising from
contracts, treaties, or laws when agreed upon by the
parties involved. Disputes are decided by an arbitral
tribunal or a conciliation commission, whose members
are typically appointed by the parties from among
international jurists worldwide. The Centre also offers
mediation and fact-finding procedures, and provides
administrative services for arbitrations conducted
under UNCITRAL and other non-ICSID frameworks.

At the core of this work are ICSID’s dispute
administration services, which cover a range of
procedures including arbitration, conciliation,
mediation, and fact-finding for disputes arising from
investment contracts, international treaties, and
domestic investment laws. ICSID’s rules and procedures
are widely regarded as the gold standard for
investment dispute settlement, offering a stable and
predictable legal framework that balances the interests
of both States and investors and has been modernized
over time to reflect best practices in the field.
ICSID also supports the development of international
investment law and dispute settlement by producing
and sharing knowledge, building capacity, and
engaging with Member States and other stakeholders
on investment dispute prevention, management,
and settlement.

Of the arbitrations concluded in fiscal 2026, 63 percent
were decided by a tribunal and 37 percent were settled
or otherwise discontinued, broadly reflecting ICSID’s
long-term trend of arbitration outcomes. Among
disputes decided by tribunals in the past year,
37 percent of awards upheld claims in part or in full,
40 percent rejected all claims on the merits, 18 percent
declined jurisdiction, and 5 percent of cases were
dismissed for manifest lack of legal merit.

Three issues of the ICSID Review – Foreign Investment Law

with Oxford University Press, the journal offers analysis
of legal developments, significant cases, and practical
issues in foreign investment law and international

FIGURE 6: ARBITRATIONS UNDER THE ICSID CONVENTION AND ADDITIONAL FACILITY
— CASES DECIDED BY TRIBUNALS IN FISCAL 2026
In ICSID arbitrations, financial compensation is
typically the primary remedy claimants seek for alleged
breaches of investment obligations. Investors typically
seek damages for harm they claim to have suffered as
a result of measures adopted by the host State. The
amounts claimed and awarded can vary significantly
depending on the nature of the investment and dispute
at issue.
In fiscal 2026, 70 percent of arbitration cases decided
by tribunals resulted in no damages awarded to
claimants, whether due to jurisdictional dismissals,
findings of no liability, or liability without damages.
Of the remaining cases, 14 percent resulted in awards
under $10 million, 8 percent in awards between
$10 million and $49 million, and 8 percent in awards
exceeding $50 million.

FIGURE 5: ICSID ADMINISTERED CASES BY FISCAL YEAR
Fiscal 2026 was a record year for ICSID. The Centre
administered 363 cases — the highest in its history —
up from 347 in fiscal 2025 and 341 in fiscal 2024. In
addition, ICSID provided services in 15 cases governed
by non-ICSID rules in fiscal 2026, 12 of which were
conducted under the UNCITRAL rules.
During fiscal 2026, ICSID registered 60 new cases —
57 arbitrations under the ICSID Convention and three
under the Additional Facility Rules — bringing the
cumulative total to 1,118 registered cases as of
June 30, 2026. On the mediation front, ICSID had
received a total of seven requests under Mediation
Rule 6 and Mediation Rule 5, with one proceeding
administered as of fiscal 2026. The year also saw 83
proceedings concluded, marking the third consecutive
fiscal year in which conclusions surpassed 80.

Working with partners around the world, ICSID delivered an extensive capacitybuilding and knowledge-sharing program on investment mediation and amicable
settlement, reaching government officials, investment promotion agencies, legal
practitioners, law students, and arbitration professionals in Asia, the Middle East,
Africa, Europe, the Americas, and the Pacific. This initiative spanned 50 events,
including 21 capacity-building sessions delivered for State officials in response to
requests from Member States and in collaboration with regional partners, reflecting a
sustained institutional commitment to advancing mediation as a credible and practical
tool for managing and amicably resolving investment disputes.

Of all
the in-person hearings in fiscal 2026, 44 percent were
held at ICSID’s hearing center in Washington, D.C., with
the remainder taking place at venues agreed upon by
the parties: Paris (30 percent), London (12 percent),
Singapore (5 percent), and other locations (9 percent).
ICSID continued to see a diverse pool of arbitrators,
conciliators, and committee members in fiscal 2026.
The Centre recorded 250 appointments to ICSID
cases, the second highest number in a single fiscal
year. Appointees represented 52 different nationalities,
and 29 percent of all appointments were nationals from
low- or middle-income economies. First-time appointees
accounted for 8 percent of all appointments; among
them, 25 percent were nationals of low- or middleincome economies and 35 percent were women.
The ICSID Secretariat comprises 76 staff members representing 39 nationalities and
speaking 22 languages, providing professional legal, administrative, and financial
services across all cases.

investment by offering an independent, specialized forum for the resolution of disputes. Effective,

GUARANTEE TRUST FUND
A notable milestone during this reporting period was
the Kingdom of Norway’s decision to join MIGA’s West
Bank and Gaza Investment Guarantee Trust Fund as a
new donor, pledging approximately $5 million over five
years. This contribution, formalized on the sidelines
of the 2025 World Bank Group–IMF Annual Meetings,
marks the first expansion of the donor base since
the trust fund’s establishment in 1997 and reflects
growing international confidence in MIGA’s ability
to operate in highly fragile environments. Norway’s
support will strengthen the fund’s capacity to provide
political risk insurance, and trade finance guarantees
in collaboration with IFC and the European Bank for
Reconstruction and Development and mobilize private
investment in the West Bank and Gaza, where elevated
risks have historically constrained capital flows. This will
help sustain economic activity, support job creation,
and advance recovery and reconstruction efforts.
MIGA EXPANDS GLOBAL

THROUGH GUARANTEES
The government of Japan and MIGA deepened a
long-standing partnership to scale up the mobilization
of private capital in developing countries. Japan
committed nearly $20 million in additional funding to
MIGA-administered trust funds, reinforcing its position
as a leading contributor and strategic partner. This
support will expand MIGA’s ability to deploy political
risk insurance and trade finance guarantees in fragile
and conflict-affected situations — including Ukraine and
the West Bank and Gaza — as well as to advance energy
transition projects in emerging and frontier markets
with a focus on Sub-Saharan Africa. The partnership
underscores Japan’s continued leadership in leveraging
innovative financing solutions through the World
Bank Group Guarantee Platform to crowd in private
investment where it is most needed and where risks
remain highest.
GUARANTEEING FINANCIAL

KATARINA ZDRALJEVIC
MIGA’S TOTAL ISSUANCE OVER $100 BILLION
MIGA was established as a member of the World Bank
Group by an international convention in April 1988,
with 29 original member countries sharing the goal
of accelerating the flow of private investment into
developing countries by insuring against political risks.
Its mission, “To promote foreign direct investment into
developing countries to support economic growth,
reduce poverty, and improve people’s lives,”
is consistent with the World Bank Group’s goals.
This fiscal year, MIGA surpassed $100 billion in
guarantees issued since its founding. With just
$366 million of paid-in capital from member countries,
MIGA has steadily pursued that mission for nearly four
decades by providing guarantees to private investors,
paving the way for private funds to flow to emerging
and developing economies, enabling job creation.

DE-RISKING THROUGH GUARANTEES
MIGA completes the World Bank Group’s integrated
approach by using trust funds to provide guarantee
instruments that de-risk investments for both public
and private sector projects. Trust funds, including the
Renewable Energy Catalyst Trust Fund, the West Bank
